Expertise refers to the perceived capability of a communicator to make accurate assertions, while trustworthiness pertains to the audience’s perception that the communicator believes in the validity of their own statements ( Hovland and Weiss, 1951 ). Many studies have proposed additional dimensions of source credibility, such as dynamism ( Berlo et al., 1969 ), authoritativeness, character ( McCroskey, 1966 ) and objectivity ( Whitehead, 1968 ). However, the precise factorial dimensions of source credibility remain a subject of ongoing debate ( Pornpitakpan, 2004 ; McCroskey and Teven, 1999 ; Hanimann et al., 2023 ). Consequently, we examined the electrophysiological signatures of source credibility during the processing of veracity cues provided by doctors for medical misinformation, focusing specifically on both perceived expertise and rating-based credibility.

The ability of source credibility to boost persuasion is a robust finding, documented across decades of behavioral research. Highly credible sources are typically more persuasive than those with low credibility (e.g., Hovland and Weiss, 1951 ; Horai et al., 1974 ; Heesacker et al., 1983 ; Pornpitakpan, 2004 ). The persuasive effects of source credibility have been extensively examined within theoretical frameworks such as the Elaboration Likelihood Model ( Cacioppo et al., 1986 ) and the Heuristic-Systematic Model ( Chaiken, 1980 ). These models posit that source credibility serves as a peripheral cue or heuristic when cognitive elaboration is low, or as a factor that enhances message scrutiny when elaboration is high. A meta-analysis by Kumkale et al. (2010) has further confirmed that persuasive effects of source credibility are robust across diverse contexts, though their magnitude varies based on message relevance and recipient involvement.

Yet, scholarly debate persists regarding which dimension of credibility exerts a dominant influence on persuasive outcomes. For example, results of Hovland and Mandell (1952) suggested that a perceived low level of trustworthiness does not necessarily reduce persuasiveness. However, McGinnies and Ward (1980) revealed that the trustworthy communicator was more influential than the untrustworthy one, whether or not he was an expert, particularly in the context of political persuasion. In clinical and public health contexts, a more granular understanding of the behavioral effects of source credibility is particularly paramount. The meta-analysis of 20 studies by Yang and Beatty (2016) indicated that expert sources have a stronger influence on perceived credibility in online health contexts compared to offline environments. The findings suggest that consumers weigh expertise more heavily when evaluating source credibility in increasingly dominant digital environments. Furthermore, Liu et al. (2022) demonstrated that in the context of health chatbots, source expertise acts as a critical heuristic cue that effectively increases usage intentions. In contrast, Lederman et al. (2014) found that when medical information is anonymous, users primarily judge credibility through social cue signaling ‘crowd consensus’.

The current study investigates the persuasive effects of medical doctors’ source credibility. Specifically, we systematically manipulated expertise — operationalized as years of work experience, a core marker of professional authority ( Ohanian, 1990 ) — and the aggregate patient star rating, which serves as the multi-dimensional peripheral trust cue most commonly encountered on online medical platforms. Importantly, within the broader literature on digital health communication, ratings are increasingly recognized as compound signals that reflect dimensions adjacent to trustworthiness, including experiential credibility, perceived reputation, and social endorsement ( Claggett et al., 2024 ; Hocevar et al., 2017 ; Metzger, 2007 ; Metzger and Flanagin, 2011 ). For instance, Han et al. (2021) showed that while consumer trust fully mediated the effect of review volume on doctor selection, it did not mediate the effect of the numerical rating.
